chief_complaint: episodic severe pain in the right upper stomach that lasts for hours after heavy meals
hpi_details: Presents with a 3-month history of distinct episodes of severe, dull, aching right upper quadrant pain occurring typically 1 to 2 hours after eating rich or creamy food. Pain builds over 30 minutes, plateaus for 2-3 hours, radiates to her right mid-back, and resolves spontaneously without residual ache. Reports three episodes this month. No fever, chills, yellow eyes, or changes in stool colour.
ideas: thinks she might have gallstones like her sister had last year
concerns: worried that an episode will happen while she is driving her children on the motorway
expectations: wants an ultrasound scan and advice on whether she needs gallbladder surgery
pmh: gestational diabetes during third pregnancy 5 years ago, obesity
social_hx: non-smoker, no alcohol intake, mother of three, part-time librarian

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Biliary Colic is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Arrange elective transabdominal ultrasound to confirm cholelithiasis, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: episodic severe pain in the right upper stomach that lasts for hours after heavy meals

Key HPI features: Presents with a 3-month history of distinct episodes of severe, dull, aching right upper quadrant pain occurring typically 1 to 2 hours after eating rich or creamy food. Pain builds over 30 minutes, plateaus for 2-3 hours, radiates to her right mid-back, and resolves spontaneously without residual ache. Reports three episodes this month. No fever, chills, yellow eyes, or changes in stool colour.

Objective/Exam findings: Abdominal exam: completely soft, non-tender in RUQ, negative Murphy's sign (as patient is between attacks). Bloods: LFTs (normal bilirubin/ALP/ALT expected), FBC, amylase. Transabdominal ultrasound scan.
Relevant background/PMH: gestational diabetes during third pregnancy 5 years ago, obesity
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Biliary Colic.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Peptic ulcer disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever or pain lasting beyond several hours without resolving — would suggest cholecystitis rather than simple colic.
management_principles: Arrange elective transabdominal ultrasound to confirm cholelithiasis
Reassure regarding normal interval examination and absence of infection
Provide dietary counseling: low-fat diet to reduce gallbladder contraction triggers
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 44F presents with recurrent episodic 2-3 hr postprandial RUQ pain radiating to right back. Spontaneous complete resolution between attacks. No pyrexia or jaundice.
reference_soap.objective: Abdominal exam: completely soft, non-tender in RUQ, negative Murphy's sign (as patient is between attacks). Bloods: LFTs (normal bilirubin/ALP/ALT expected), FBC, amylase. Transabdominal ultrasound scan.
reference_soap.assessment: Biliary colic due to cholelithiasis without cholecystitis or ductal obstruction. DDx: peptic ulcer disease, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, functional dyspepsia, sphincter of Oddi dysfunction.
reference_soap.plan: Arrange elective transabdominal ultrasound to confirm cholelithiasis. Reassure regarding normal interval examination and absence of infection. Provide dietary counseling: low-fat diet to reduce gallbladder contraction triggers. Analgesia prescription (NSAIDs e.g. diclofenac/ibuprofen or paracetamol PRN for attacks). Refer to general surgery for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

learning_objectives: Differentiate biliary colic from acute cholecystitis based on episodic duration (<6 hours) and complete inter-attack resolution
Recognise the classic biliary pain pattern plateau and crescendo mechanics
Provide evidence-based dietary modifications to minimize cholecystokinin-mediated gallbladder contractions
Outline the pathway for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy and red flags requiring emergency return

teaching.one_liner: A gallstone temporarily blocks the gallbladder outlet after a fatty meal, causing steady right-upper-quadrant pain that builds, plateaus, and then fully resolves.
red_flags: Fever or pain lasting beyond several hours without resolving — would suggest cholecystitis rather than simple colic

must_ask.say: Does the pain start an hour or two after eating rich or fatty food?
Does the pain go away completely on its own after a few hours, without leaving any ache?
Does it spread through to your shoulder blade or the middle of your back?
Have you had any fevers or chills with these episodes?
Have you noticed any yellowing of your skin or eyes, or a change in stool colour?
How many of these episodes have you had, and how often?
